newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIA POLITICS IN TURMOIL AS LEFT CLAIMS WIN.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIA POLITICS IN TURMOIL AS LEFT CLAIMS WIN.

text.p: Albania's fragmented political scene was turned on its head after right-leaning President Sali Berisha conceded defeat in a general election at the weekend to his key rivals, the Socialists.

Sunday's poll, the fourth multi-party election since the country emerged from almost half a century of Stalinist isolation in 1990, was endorsed by international observers as "adequate and acceptable".
Berisha's Democrats have dominated Albanian politics since they swept to power in 1992. The party won a crushing majority in last year's general election widely considered as flawed.

The Socialists, led by Fatos Nano who was released from prison only three months ago, claimed even before the first official results came trickling in that they had won almost two-thirds of seats in the new parliament.
Unusually frequent volleys of gunfire broke out around central Tirana late on Monday, despite a 10 p.m. to 5 a.m curfew, lifted only for election day, still being in force.
A Reuter correspondent saw armoured vehicles, police vans and ambulances pass through the square, but there were no immediate reports of casualties.
The interior ministry maintained a ban on demonstrations in Tirana pending publication of results but an authorised Socialist rally was scheduled for Tuesday in Tirana.
Emergency measures were imposed on March 2, at the height of a wave of violence sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes which has left at least 1,500 people dead.

Celebratory gunfire also resounded throughout the country's anarchic south, focus of the armed unrest. An Italian soldier, part of the multinational protection force despatched to help restore order, was badly wounded in shooting in the Adriatic port of Vlore and was flown to Italy for emergency treatment.
Berisha appeared to confirm early reports of a crushing Socialist victory, but said nothing about quitting.

"Albanian voters yesterday seemingly voted that the Democratic Party should be in opposition. On this occasion I would like to express my deepest gratitude to those hundreds and thousands of Albanians...who supported the Democratic Party," a relaxed-looking Berisha said on state television.
He urged members and sympathisers of his party "to treat yesterday's verdict with courage and dignity."
Democratic Party chairman Tritan Shehu said: "He has not resigned for the moment. But it all depends on him now."

Catherine Lalumiere, the top official observing the election under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said the vote had showed Albanians' desire for a democratic future despite minor flaws.

"We believe therefore that we can say that the elections can be considered as adequate and acceptable," she said. "The result of these elections can be the foundation for a stable, democratic system, which Albanians want and deserve."

The OSCE, together with other European and U.S. observers, monitored Sunday's first round of the election. The head of the OSCE mission, former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, was due in Albania for talks with political leaders on Tuesday.

Albania's election commission announced official returns in 11 of the country's 115 constituencies -- seven captured by Socialists and their allies and four going to run-off rounds next week after none of the candidates cleared 50 percent.
Election officials had already announced Socialist victories in some southern regions.
A two-thirds majority would be enough to remove a head of state by parliamentary vote. Berisha has hinted on several occasions that he would quit if the left came to power.
